record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: How can human genetic studies overcome the overrepresentation of European ancestry by collecting diverse cohorts and developing robust trans-ethnic analytical methods, so that genetic associations and polygenic risk scores transfer across populations and causal signals can be distinguished from population-specific confounding or linkage disequilibrium?

evidence.quote: The absence of ethnic diversity in genetic studies is hard to overemphasize (open problem #7: ethnic diversity). Individuals of European ancestry are overwhelmingly overrepresented in contemporary cohorts and, as a result, most published results do not directly transfer to other ethnic groups

the replication of a genetic association across multiple ethnicities is strong evidence for causality. In addition to more diverse datasets and increased awareness by researchers, there is also need for better analytical methods for robust analysis of trans-ethnic cohorts

haplotype reference panels are highly biased towards individuals of European ancestry, and so are the popular DNA microarrays (which usually genotype variants present in these populations). As a result, the genetic coverage obtained for non-Europeans is typically much lower (open problem #7: ethnic diversity).

artifact.category_tag: trans-ethnic genetic association and polygenic risk scores
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the statistical genetics setting in which one collects genome-wide genotype data and a quantitative or binary phenotype from cohorts of individuals drawn from several ancestral populations P_1, ..., P_K (e.g., European, African, East Asian, South Asian, admixed American). For each population P_k one obtains a sample of (X^{(k)}, y^{(k)}) where X^{(k)} \in \{0,1,2\}^{n_k \times M} encodes minor-allele dosages at M variants and y^{(k)} \in \R^{n_k} encodes phenotypes. Genetic association studies typically fit per-variant marginal models or joint linear/logistic models to obtain effect-size estimates \hat{\beta}^{(k)} \in \R^M, and polygenic risk scores (PRS) are defined for an individual with genotype vector x as PRS(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} w_j x_j for weights w derived from \hat{\beta}. Empirically, when weights w are estimated from a European-ancestry cohort and applied to individuals of non-European ancestry, predictive accuracy (e.g., R^2 between PRS and phenotype) drops substantially, due to differences in allele frequencies, linkage-disequilibrium (LD) patterns \Sigma^{(k)} = \Cov(X^{(k)}), causal effect heterogeneity, and population-specific confounding.

Formulate and solve the following problem. Develop a framework, together with cohort-design and analytical methodology, that:

(a) Specifies a generative model linking population-specific LD matrices \Sigma^{(k)}, allele frequencies f^{(k)}, and (possibly shared) causal effects \beta^* such that observed marginal effects \hat{\beta}^{(k)} can be related across populations.

(b) Provides an estimator \hat{w} of PRS weights, using multi-ancestry training data, for which the cross-population predictive performance gap
\Delta(k, k') = \E[(y - \mathrm{PRS}_{\hat{w}}(x))^2 \mid \text{ancestry } k'] - \E[(y - \mathrm{PRS}_{\hat{w}}(x))^2 \mid \text{ancestry } k]
is provably bounded under explicit assumptions on the heterogeneity of \beta^*, \Sigma^{(k)}, and f^{(k)}.

(c) Provides a hypothesis-testing procedure that distinguishes, at a given variant or locus, between (i) a genuine shared causal effect, (ii) a population-specific causal effect, and (iii) a spurious association arising from LD tagging or population stratification, with controlled type-I error across all K populations simultaneously.

(d) Quantifies the minimal sample sizes n_1, ..., n_K (in particular for currently underrepresented non-European ancestries) and the required density and ancestry-coverage of haplotype reference panels and genotyping arrays needed to attain a prescribed cross-ancestry transferability of association signals and PRS accuracy.

The goal is a complete, rigorous solution: an analytical methodology with provable guarantees, together with cohort-design recommendations, that achieves trans-ethnic transferability of genetic association results and polygenic risk scores while distinguishing causal signals from population-specific confounding and LD artifacts.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broadly recognized open challenge in statistical and human genetics. Recent literature (multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis methods such as MR-MEGA, trans-ethnic PRS methods like PRS-CSx, and ongoing initiatives such as H3Africa, All of Us, and the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative) has produced substantial partial progress, but cross-ancestry PRS portability gaps and the lack of representative reference panels and arrays remain unresolved as of 2026. No comprehensive solution meeting all aspects (a)-(d) exists.

status_evidence.title: Polygenic prediction across populations: PRS-CSx
status_evidence.snippet: Improvements in cross-ancestry polygenic prediction; gaps remain for non-European populations.
status_evidence.claim: Cross-ancestry PRS portability has improved but remains substantially worse for non-European ancestries, indicating the problem is only partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative
status_evidence.snippet: Multi-ancestry biobank meta-analysis effort to improve trans-ethnic genetic discovery.
status_evidence.claim: Active ongoing initiatives confirm the open status of trans-ethnic methodology and cohort representation.

status_evidence.title: The missing diversity in human genetic studies (Sirugo et al., Cell 2019; updates through 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Documents persistent overrepresentation of European-ancestry participants and resulting transferability problems.
status_evidence.claim: The diversity gap and transferability problem are widely cited as open.
